report.summary: QGIS merges QEP428, banning all LLM, AI, and agent-assisted code contributions, replacing its earlier human-in-the-loop AI policy with a total prohibition.
report.background: QGIS is one of the world's most widely used open-source geographic information systems, with a long-standing community of volunteer and corporate contributors. Like many large projects, it first tried a permissive approach: QEP-408, adapted from LLVM's AI Tool Use Policy, required contributors to review all LLM output, disclose assistance through an 'Assisted-by' trailer, and forbade unreviewed agent-generated comments. In practice, maintainers found that process was widely ignored, and the project reports losing at least one extremely high-value contributor over AI-related friction. Amid a broader 2026 open-source backlash against low-quality AI-generated patches, core contributor Nyall Dawson proposed QEP428, an outright ban with sanctions for violators, framed explicitly as starting with a closed door that could be selectively opened later for narrow uses such as autocomplete or translation.
key_points: QEP428 states plainly that no LLM, AI, or agent-assisted code contributions are allowed in the qgis/qgis repository, and that discovered violations may lead to code reversion and sanctions on contributor rights.
The ban replaces QEP-408, an LLVM-inspired policy that permitted AI assistance if fully reviewed and disclosed. Dawson argued that policy's safeguards 'clearly didn't happen in reality'.
The proposal passed its discussion period on October 5, moved to a vote, and was merged into the QGIS Enhancement Proposals repository on October 7 after authoring by core contributor Nyall Dawson.
The door is not permanently shut: discussion indicates the project may later reopen narrowly defined cases, such as AI used as an autocomplete replacement or for translation work.
QGIS joins a growing list of open-source projects drawing hard lines on AI-generated code, driven less by ideology than by maintainer review burden and contributor trust.
report.impact: For the AI industry, QGIS is a signal that a major, respectable scientific open-source project judges current AI contribution norms to be net-negative, contradicting vendors' narrative that AI-assisted coding is universally welcomed. For developers, it means Copilot, Cursor, and agent workflows are effectively off-limits for QGIS patches, and the sanction language — reversion plus contributor-rights penalties — raises the stakes for disclosure. It also pressures other projects to pick a side, likely producing a split landscape of AI-friendly and AI-restricted repositories. For regular users, the practical near-term effect is neutral to positive: maintainers argue the ban protects code quality and prevents volunteer burnout, though QGIS may lose some productivity gains from willing AI users.
report.tools: Readers can examine the QEP428 text and prior QEP-408 in the QGIS-Enhancement-Proposals repository on GitHub, and compare LLVM's AI Tool Use Policy, which inspired the earlier rules, along with AI-contribution policies from Gentoo, NetBSD, and Fedora. For disclosure experiments, the 'Assisted-by' git trailer convention and GitHub Copilot's code-referencing settings are worth tracking. To try QGIS itself, download the open-source desktop app and its plugin ecosystem.
